title: From Temple to study
hookLine: at Yavneh, Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuilds Jewish life around study and prayer
last: ALL LOOKING AT THE SAME ROCK.

lines: A COFFIN AT THE CITY GATE.
HE WALKS TO THE ROMAN TENT.
cards: The coffin is carried to the city gate by two students, one at the head and one at the feet. The guards want to stab it, to be sure the body is dead. The students talk them out of it.
Inside the coffin is their teacher, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, very much alive. That's how the Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells his escape from the besieged city.
He has pretended to be sick, then pretended to die, because the zealots holding Jerusalem won't let anyone leave. Once outside, he walks to the Roman commander's tent with one request.

teach.h: GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.
teach.b: In the Talmud's story the Roman is Vespasian, soon to become emperor, and he tells the rabbi to ask him for something. Among his requests, Rabbi Yochanan asks, in paraphrase: give me Yavneh and its sages. Not Jerusalem.
Not the Temple. A place to keep teaching. The Talmud doesn't pretend everyone agreed.

teach.h: SOME SAID HE SHOULD HAVE ASKED MORE.
teach.b: It records a sharp objection, that he should have asked Rome to spare Jerusalem itself, and it gives his reasoning: ask for that much, and he might not get even a little rescue. Think what had just been lost.

Jewish worship had a center: one house, one altar, priests, offerings. With the Temple burned, what could take its place? At Yavneh, tradition says, the sages began to answer: study of Torah, and prayer.
The Talmud links the daily prayers to the daily Temple offerings, so the words a person says stand where the offering once stood.

Long before, the prophet Hosea had pointed this way: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." The same verse ends with an offering of a new kind; in the Hebrew, it is bulls of our lips. Words, in place of bulls.
A sanctuary made of time and speech, which can be carried anywhere. In the rabbis' telling, that move, from Temple to study, is how a people without a Temple kept going. The house was gone.

how: Jewish prayer services follow a daily rhythm that the Talmud connects to the Temple offerings, and Torah study, in a synagogue, a study hall or at home, is itself treated as a form of worship.

games.q: you're Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai in the Roman tent. the commander tells you to ask him for something. what do you ask for?
o: give me Yavneh and its sages.
let me go home in peace.
games.why: he asks for Yavneh and its sages. the Talmud records the objection that he should have asked for Jerusalem, and his answer: ask for too much and you may get nothing.

practice: Choose something that changed and can't go back to the way it was: a job, a home, a friendship, a way your body used to work.
Then ask Rabbi Yochanan's question, not how do I get the whole city back, but what is my Yavneh: one small thing I can still build, here, that carries what mattered.
If you pray, you can take with you words, as Hosea says, and return.

wordCard.voice: Yavneh. The town Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asked Rome for, where Jewish life was rebuilt around Torah study and prayer after the Temple fell.
